attributes.title: AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking
attributes.summary: A word of caution on this study: The questionnaire they use does not actually test critical thinking skills but asks Likert-scale questions *about* people's critical thinking skills. Self-reported measurements at this scale is still interesting, especially paired with the qualitative interviews, but the abstract should probably say *reported* AI tool usage and critical thinking abilities, and probably shouldn't use the term "scores."
attributes.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools has transformed numerous aspects of daily life, yet its impact on critical thinking remains underexplored. This study investigates the relationship between AI tool usage and critical thinking skills, focusing on cognitive offloading as a mediating factor. Utilising a mixed-method approach, we conducted surveys and in-depth interviews with 666 participants across diverse age groups and educational backgrounds. Quantitative data were analysed using ANOVA and correlation analysis, while qualitative insights were obtained through thematic analysis of interview transcripts. The findings revealed a significant negative correlation between frequent AI tool usage and critical thinking abilities, mediated by increased cognitive offloading. Younger participants exhibited higher dependence on AI tools and lower critical thinking scores compared to older participants. Furthermore, higher educational attainment was associated with better critical thinking skills, regardless of AI usage. These results highlight the potential cognitive costs of AI tool reliance, emphasising the need for educational strategies that promote critical engagement with AI technologies. This study contributes to the growing discourse on AI’s cognitive implications, offering practical recommendations for mitigating its adverse effects on critical thinking. The findings underscore the importance of fostering critical thinking in an AI-driven world, making this research essential reading for educators, policymakers, and technologists.

nodes.label: Agency does not equal choice – conceptualizing agency for learning in the age of AI

attributes.title: Agency does not equal choice – conceptualizing agency for learning in the age of AI
attributes.summary:
Interesting three-part view of agency in the context of student learners. The author argues that agency is more than just who makes the choice; it breaks down into:
1. The opportunity for self-direction, e.g., a student picking their avatar or choosing what module to study. The effects of self-direction is often measured with "yoked" designs where one learner watches another use technology (e.g., make choices); studies show that the positive effects of self-direction increase with age.
2. The opportunity to make decisions about learning, e.g., young children can tell if problems are easy or hard, but only older children allocate more time to studying hard ones.
3. The opportunity to enact decisions, i.e., metacognitive control, e.g., when students decide what content to go back and review.

nodes.label: Can you help me? Using others to offload cognition

attributes.title: Can you help me? Using others to offload cognition
attributes.summary: One of those papers that shows empirically what we know inherently – people change how much they offload to other people depending on their perception of those people's competence. For the Guide's purpose, it's worth keeping in mind: If this is our tendency, then how we perceive machines will affect how much we rely on them. (There was also an interesting section on sex differences: Women offloaded earlier in the second phase if they did poorly in the first phase, while this wasn't as pronounced for men; and women offloaded on both male and female helpers, while men were significantly more likely to offload on female helpers. This, too, feels relevant to LLM assistant design.)
attributes.abstract: One of the most ancient and widely used forms of cognitive offloading is the outsourcing of cognitive operations onto other humans. Here, we explore whether humans preferentially seek out and use information from more competent compared with less competent others in an ongoing cognitive task. Participants (N = 120) completed a novel computerised visuospatial working memory task where each trial required them to remember either one, five, or ten target locations and recall them after a brief delay. Next, participants watched two virtual people compete in a distinct memory game, where one performed relatively well, demonstrating a stronger memory, and the other performed relatively poorly, demonstrating a weaker memory. Finally, participants completed the initial memory task again, but this time, either the strong-memory person or the weak-memory person was available to help with recall on each trial. Our results showed that, through observation and without direct instruction, participants acquired beliefs about the virtual people's cognitive proficiencies and could readily draw upon these beliefs to inform offloading decisions. Participants were typically more likely to ask for help from the strong-memory person, and this tendency was independent from other factors known to drive cognitive offloading more generally, like task difficulty, unaided cognitive ability, and metacognitive confidence.

nodes.label: Beyond the Singularity Myth: Artificial General Intelligence as Cumulative Infrastructural Transformation—Absorption Capacity, Epistemic Drift, and the Erosion of Human Verification Power

attributes.title: Beyond the Singularity Myth: Artificial General Intelligence as Cumulative Infrastructural Transformation—Absorption Capacity, Epistemic Drift, and the Erosion of Human Verification Power
attributes.summary:
This piece is written by the Chief AI Officer of GMU. He argues that, rather than worry about some single moment of AGI, the concern is the "cumulative handover of decision-making authority to systems whose reasoning we can no longer fully trace, verify, or override." Shehu opens with a description of the experiments they did at GMU, from AI tutors and syllabi writers to AI secretaries and admissions staff. He points out that, while these experiments are disconnected and early, they are happening everywhere; his concern is that AIs are becoming infrastructural, critical actors embedded in critical workflows, while discourse still argues about whether AGI has "happened."

Shehu defines the "absorption gap, that widening space between technological capability and human capacity to meaningfully oversee, verify and steer autonomous systems," as being made up of three components:

1. Governance lag, where our systems operate on timespans of months to years (e.g., a university's curriculum revision occurs every few years) while a new model capability can deploy "overnight." This means governing institutions fall farther behind and become more risk-averse, while product companies make key decisions about how people use AI.
2. Institutional misalignment, where, even if we could accurately align models, the result would be models aligned to fragments of systems, acting with unpredictable consequences. Shehu argues that alignment is a political problem more than a technical one.
3. Capability inequality, the fear that those with access to and knowledge about how to use AI will pull farther ahead. Shehu argues that we must ensure that public institutions (schools, government agencies, etc.) can absorb AI – meaning teacher training, public compute, etc.

Shehu closes with a fourth worry that I'll highlight here because I think it is well-put: "As models become more complex if not more capable, they increasingly operate in high-dimensional latent spaces that are fundamentally inaccessible to human inspection. We can observe inputs and outputs. We can measure performance. But we cannot trace the reasoning path from one to the other...The system works, or appears to work, but we cannot explain why, and therefore cannot predict when it will fail." He calls this *epistemic drift* towards a world where verification is no longer possible, and the corresponding *epistemic authority* the ability to retain governance and understanding of the behavior of AI systems.<Footnote>Shehu also makes some suggestions as to how to build governance systems and AI literacy to ensure this authority, but I found them too vague to add to this summary. Do check out the piece if you're interested.</Footnote>
attributes.abstract: The dominant framing of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) as a discrete breakthrough obscures the more urgent reality: AGI is arriving as a gradual, cumulative erosion of human verification power distributed across institutions and decision-making systems. This article reframes the AGI transition through the lens of absorption capacity; that is, the rate at which human systems can integrate, govern, and maintain meaningful oversight of increasingly autonomous AI. Drawing on empirical observations from deploying enterprise-scale generative AI in a large public university and personal experiences as a long-standing AI researcher and educator, in this article, I identify three critical asymmetries characterizing this transition: (1) governance lag, where policy cycles cannot match technological iteration speed; (2) institutional misalignment, where locally rational AI systems produce collectively irrational societal outcomes; and (3) capability inequality, where uneven access to AI amplifies structural advantage. I argue that the defining challenge is not achieving technical alignment with human values, but maintaining epistemic authority, which is the human capacity to verify, understand, and steer systems reasoning in latent spaces beyond direct audit. The article concludes that the true measure of preparedness for AGI is not computational power or algorithmic sophistication, but adaptive governance: institutional architectures capable of co-evolving with the technologies they must regulate. The frontier is not artificial superintelligence. It is collective human capacity to remain intelligible to ourselves while embedded in AI-mediated decision ecosystems.
attributes.publication: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology

nodes.label: Report from Workshop on Dialogue alongside Artificial Intelligence

attributes.title: Report from Workshop on Dialogue alongside Artificial Intelligence
attributes.summary:
This report is from a workshop held to discuss how AI should be used in education and, specifically, dialogic education.<Footnote>Note: Not chat interface dialogue but dialogue as a pedagogical and human practice, e.g., making an argument about something to someone and listening to their response.</Footnote> The authors start with the main concern: That AI is both useful *and* potentially detrimental not only to students' cognitive agency but to the "human element" of education. On the "useful" side, the authors note presentations on AI for analyzing classroom discourse; projects using AI to train both students and teachers in dialogic practices; various kinds of AI coaches for teachers; and an early project, "Chat-with-CAT," on a chatbot that helps students refine arguments. On the "cautionary" side, participants pointed out that having LLMs act as coaches for argument-building requires us to decide first whether objective answers exist. Similarly, the authors recorded concerns about the fine line between critical brainstorming and overreliance; student agency as sense-maker rather than answer-accepter; a decline in class discussions and collaboration between students; access and achievement gaps; and risks to the relational and human aspects of dialogue, and corresponding degradation of communication skills.

The general agreement from the workshop was that "AI should not function autonomously in high-stakes decision-making or interaction without human oversight." There were many examples of this, e.g., having an AI mediator during student dialogues, but I felt their reassurance of "human in the loop" was an overpromise. They also recommended domain-specific AI (e.g., using a RAG system tied to the curriculum), implementing scaffolding (i.e., systems that give fewer and more high-level hints as the student learns), and transparency in how systems work, including why they provide the content they do. The authors emphasized the need for longitudinal impact studies, cross-cultural validation, and a range of other work you can check out in their conclusions section.
attributes.abstract: Educational dialogue -- the collaborative exchange of ideas through talk -- is widely recognized as a catalyst for deeper learning and critical thinking in and across contexts. At the same time, artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly emerged as a powerful force in education, with the potential to address major challenges, personalize learning, and innovate teaching practices. However, these advances come with significant risks: rapid AI development can undermine human agency, exacerbate inequities, and outpace our capacity to guide its use with sound policy. Human learning presupposes cognitive efforts and social interaction (dialogues). In response to this evolving landscape, an international workshop titled "Educational Dialogue: Moving Thinking Forward" convened 19 leading researchers from 11 countries in Cambridge (September 1-3, 2025) to examine the intersection of AI and educational dialogue. This AI-focused strand of the workshop centered on three critical questions: (1) When is AI truly useful in education, and when might it merely replace human effort at the expense of learning? (2) Under what conditions can AI use lead to better dialogic teaching and learning? (3) Does the AI-human partnership risk outpacing and displacing human educational work, and what are the implications? These questions framed two days of presentations and structured dialogue among participants.

nodes.label: Does using artificial intelligence assistance accelerate skill decay and hinder skill development without performers’ awareness?

attributes.title: Does using artificial intelligence assistance accelerate skill decay and hinder skill development without performers’ awareness?
attributes.summary: This paper puts forward the hypothesis that AI will increase skill decay (though does not test these hypotheses empirically.) The authors note precedence in the automation literature: While automation can make otherwise exhausting tasks doable, like piloting a long flight, it can also lead to reliance and worse performance when automation is absent. On top of that, skill decay occurs more readily with tasks that require greater cognitive effort and less physical involvement, including subtasks, e.g., landing a plan versus maintaining awareness of a plane's location. The authors argue that because AI systems are designed to replace work that requires cognitive effort with next to no physical involvement, intending to assist with decision-making that was "previously the expert's domain alone," experts who use AI frequently are at high risk of skill decay that they may or may not be aware of. They lay out a set of research questions for fields to follow up on.
attributes.abstract: Artificial intelligence in the workplace is becoming increasingly common. These tools are sometimes used to aid users in performing their task, for example, when an artificial intelligence tool assists a radiologist in their search for abnormalities in radiographic images. The use of artificial intelligence brings a wealth of benefits, such as increasing the efficiency and efficacy of performance. However, little research has been conducted to determine how the use of artificial intelligence assistants might affect the user's cognitive skills. In this theoretical perspective, we discuss how artificial intelligence assistants might accelerate skill decay among experts and hinder skill acquisition among learners. Further, we discuss how AI assistants might also prevent experts and learners from recognizing these deleterious effects. We then discuss the types of questions: use-inspired basic cognitive researchers, applied researchers, and computer science researchers should seek to answer. We conclude that multidisciplinary research from use-inspired basic cognitive research, domain-specific applied research, and technical research (e.g., human factors research, computer science research) is needed to (a) understand these potential consequences, (b) design artificial intelligence systems to mitigate these impacts, and (c) develop training and use protocols to prevent negative impacts on users' cognitive skills. Only by answering these questions from multidisciplinary perspectives can we harness the benefits of artificial intelligence in the workplace while preventing negative impacts on users' cognitive skills.

nodes.label: AI Makes You Smarter, But None The Wiser: The Disconnect Between Performance and Metacognition

attributes.title: AI Makes You Smarter, But None The Wiser: The Disconnect Between Performance and Metacognition
attributes.summary:
This paper is concerned with metacognition specifically in the context of confidence – are we able to accurately assess our own competence in situations where we use AI? They specifically examine the Dunning-Kruger effect, a "cognitive bias where individuals with lower ability overestimate their competence while those with higher ability underestimate it." They do two studies (N of 246 and 452, respectively) where they asked participants to use AI to work LSAT problems, then asked them to do self-assessments. The authors find that AI improves performance on LSAT problems but also leads to overestimation of performance across the board (i.e., the Dunning-Kruger effect disappears because high performers also overestimate their performance.) They conclude that AI use affects metacognitive monitoring – and, worse, whether the AI was being used as an oracle or a teammate did not seem to affect participants' assessment accuracy. 

One weird and relevant thing the authors found was that people with higher AI literacy were actually *less* accurate in their self-assessments (something that runs counter to suggestions that AI literacy be [increased](node:ebf5c6bd-02fc-4ecf-9b79-08fd3ad8a45a) and [other findings](node:041f9130-cf74-4065-9742-cd53b2591648) that information literacy reduces negative effects from AI dependence.) That is, just because you know how AI works doesn't mean you're accurate in your assessment of how you work with AI. But, of course, AI literacy was self-reported and so could easily be biased.
attributes.abstract: People are not able to accurately assess their performance when using AI. Large Language Model usage levels out the Dunning--Kruger effect. Higher AI literacy correlates with lower self-assessment accuracy. Higher confidence correlates with lower self-assessment accuracy. LLM use improves human reasoning performance in the Law School Admission Test.

attributes.description: Metacognition is our ability to monitor and regulate our own cognitive processes (see [Flavell](node:43e4c387-80eb-4307-bc35-e4fdec216d6a) for the OG paper.)
Cognitive fatigue is when we lose the ability to think and focus, often caused by informational overload or prolonged mental activity.
This category groups information by its relevant domain: AI in education, AI in software engineering, etc.
What people use to evaluate human cognition, problem-solving and other aspects in the context of AI.
Self-assessment of AI literacy

nodes.label: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics

attributes.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
attributes.abstract: Generative AI is poised to revolutionize how humans work, and has already demonstrated promise in significantly improving human productivity. A key question is how generative AI affects learning-namely, how humans acquire new skills as they perform tasks. Learning is critical to long-term productivity, especially since generative AI is fallible and users must check its outputs. We study this question via a field experiment where we provide nearly a thousand high school math students with access to generative AI tutors. To understand the differential impact of tool design on learning, we deploy two generative AI tutors: one that mimics a standard ChatGPT interface ("GPT Base") and one with prompts designed to safeguard learning ("GPT Tutor"). Consistent with prior work, our results show that having GPT-4 access while solving problems significantly improves performance (48% improvement in grades for GPT Base and 127% for GPT Tutor). However, we additionally find that when access is subsequently taken away, students actually perform worse than those who never had access (17% reduction in grades for GPT Base)-i.e., unfettered access to GPT-4 can harm educational outcomes. These negative learning effects are largely mitigated by the safeguards in GPT Tutor. Without guardrails, students attempt to use GPT-4 as a "crutch" during practice problem sessions, and subsequently perform worse on their own. Thus, decision-makers must be cautious about design choices underlying generative AI deployments to preserve skill learning and long-term productivity.
attributes.publication: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

attributes.title: The last astronomers
attributes.summary: A fascinating article on the different views of astrophysicists on AI and their field. From being "left behind" to wanting to preserve the social process of science to the purpose and meaning of human inquiry into the universe, would recommend as a short but moving read.
attributes.abstract: Amid a flood of AI advances, astrophysicists are questioning the soul of their field.

nodes.label: Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring

attributes.title: Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring
attributes.summary: This is a puzzling study! The headline finding is really that kids did *not* use an AI literacy platform, although they used it *slightly* more when paired with a human tutor. The baffling thing is that the authors don't discuss why or what the kids were doing otherwise during the time set aside for platform engagement...but it's a finding that was replicated in the big [Hamilton County Khanmigo study](node:9c8e90c1-ca73-4298-bbbd-aac78c53559c), so engagement is clearly a problem.
attributes.abstract: AI tutoring platforms offer a promising path to scaling personalized instruction, but only if students use them. We report findings from two randomized controlled trials in which elementary students were assigned to use an AI literacy platform independently or with an in-person tutor focused on engagement, not direct instruction. Despite dedicated session time, nearly half of students in the control group never used the platform, and those who did averaged only 2-5 minutes per week. Working with human tutors increased average weekly platform usage by 1 to 4 minutes and engagement by 71-80%. However, usage remained low, and the intervention did not improve reading achievement. Findings suggest that access alone is insufficient; implementation and human support matter for promoting meaningful engagement with AI-based learning tools.

nodes.label: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise

attributes.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
attributes.abstract: Generative AI, particularly Language Models (LMs), has the potential to transform real-world domains with societal impact, particularly where access to experts is limited. For example, in education, training novice educators with expert guidance is important for effectiveness but expensive, creating significant barriers to improving education quality at scale. This challenge disproportionately hurts students from under-served communities, who stand to gain the most from high-quality education and are most likely to be taught by inexperienced educators. We introduce Tutor CoPilot, a novel Human-AI approach that leverages a model of expert thinking to provide expert-like guidance to tutors as they tutor. This study presents the first randomized controlled trial of a Human-AI system in live tutoring, involving 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students from historically under-served communities. Following a preregistered analysis plan, we find that students working on mathematics with tutors randomly assigned to have access to Tutor CoPilot are 4 percentage points (p.p.) more likely to master topics (p<0.01). Notably, students of lower-rated tutors experienced the greatest benefit, improving mastery by 9 p.p. relative to the control group. We find that Tutor CoPilot costs only $20 per-tutor annually, based on the tutors’ usage during the study. We analyze 550,000+ messages using classifiers to identify pedagogical strategies, and find that tutors with access to Tutor CoPilot are more likely to use strategies that foster student understanding (e.g., asking guiding questions) and less likely to give away the answer to the student, aligning with high-quality teaching practices. Tutor interviews qualitatively highlight how Tutor CoPilot’s guidance helps them to respond to student needs, though tutors flag common issues in Tutor CoPilot, such as generating suggestions that are not grade-level appropriate. Altogether, our study of Tutor CoPilot demonstrates how Human-AI systems can scale expertise in real-world domains in real time, bridge gaps in skills and create a future where high-quality education is accessible to all students.

nodes.label: One Click Away: AI Tutoring with Khanmigo in a Two-Year School Experiment

attributes.title: One Click Away: AI Tutoring with Khanmigo in a Two-Year School Experiment
attributes.abstract: Generative AI has been promoted as the technology that could transform education by providing every student a personal tutor. We provide some of the first large-scale experimental evidence, from a two-year cluster randomized trial in 18 Tennessee middle schools in which randomly assigned students used Khan Academy with its AI tutor, Khanmigo, configured to coach rather than give answers, during existing daily remedial mathematics sessions. Assignment raises math achievement by 1.3 national percentile ranks per term, or about 0.06 to 0.08 standard deviations over a school year; the implied effect of a full year of active participation reaches 0.14 standard deviations. These gains resemble those from Khan Academy practice without AI assistance. One explanation is that students used the tutor infrequently and, when they did, rarely engaged it in substantive mathematical dialogue: 96 percent of students tried Khanmigo at least once, but the median student messaged it on only a third of the days they practiced, and in only 17 percent of the exercise sessions in which they made a mistake. Messages that students did send were mostly bare answers or clicks on suggested prompts. The binding constraint appears to be engagement: realizing the promise of AI tutoring will require getting students to use it, not just giving them access.

nodes.label: Automated feedback improves teachers’ questioning quality in brick-and-mortar classrooms: Opportunities for further enhancement

attributes.title: Automated feedback improves teachers’ questioning quality in brick-and-mortar classrooms: Opportunities for further enhancement
attributes.abstract: AI-powered professional learning tools that provide teachers with individualized feedback on their instruction have proven effective at improving instruction and student engagement in virtual learning contexts. Despite the need for consistent, personalized professional learning in K-12 settings, the effectiveness of automated feedback tools in traditional classrooms remains unexplored. We present results from 224 Utah mathematics and science teachers who engaged in a pre-registered randomized controlled trial, conducted in partnership with TeachFX, to assess the impact of automated feedback in K-12 classrooms. This feedback targeted “focusing questions” — questions that probe students’ thinking by pressing for explanations and reflection. We find that teachers opened emails containing the automated feedback about 53–65% of the time, and the feedback increased their use of focusing questions by 20% (p < 0.01) compared to the control group. The feedback did not impact other teaching practices. Qualitative interviews with 13 teachers revealed mixed perceptions of the automated feedback. Some teachers appreciated the reflective insights, while others faced barriers such as skepticism about accuracy, data privacy concerns, and time constraints. Our findings highlight the promises and areas of improvement for implementing effective and teacher-friendly automated professional learning tools in brick-and-mortar classrooms.

nodes.label: Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: A Large-Scale Study of Feedback Workflows and Student Enactment

attributes.title: Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: A Large-Scale Study of Feedback Workflows and Student Enactment
attributes.abstract: Feedback processes strongly influence student learning, yet realising their educational potential requires addressing two distinct barriers: providing high-quality, timely, and individualised feedback comments at scale, and supporting students to interpret, evaluate, and act on those comments productively. Generative AI offers a credible means of addressing the provision barrier, with growing evidence that AI-generated feedback comments can be pedagogically comparable to educator-generated feedback comments. However, students’ uptake remains limited, making productive feedback use a critical constraint on the educational value of AI-generated feedback comments. We conducted a large-scale quasi-experimental sequential cohort study comparing three AI-mediated feedback workflows across 13,037 students, 51,296 student-authored resources, and 70 course offerings. In Directed Feedback (n = 3,723), students received AI-generated feedback comments without structured support. In Self-Directed Feedback (n = 3,951), students could initiate optional AI-supported dialogue. In Enacted Feedback (n = 5,363), the workflow prompted students to select feedback suggestions, evaluate their relevance, and engage in targeted AI-supported dialogue anchored to those selections. Enacted Feedback was associated with significantly higher uptake of AI-generated feedback comments, with an estimated probability of 26.2%, compared with 14.1% for Directed Feedback and 0.1% for Self-Directed Feedback. It was also associated with significantly higher self-assessment confidence and submitted-work quality than both comparison conditions. These findings suggest that the educational value of AI-generated feedback depends not only on the quality of feedback comments, but also on AI-mediated feedback workflows that actively structure students’ enactment of feedback literacy processes. The paper discusses implications for the design of AI feedback systems that position learners not as passive recipients of feedback comments, but as active participants in processes of judgement, dialogue, and improvement.

nodes.label: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting

attributes.title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
attributes.summary:
People were understandably stunned at this outcome! The AI tutor the study used was prompt-based, with sequential explanations of the lessons included. The authors found that the amount of time students spent with the AI tutor corresponded with whether they had felt the classroom lesson was too fast or too slow. Possibly most interesting is they found motivation and engagement were higher for the AI tutor than the in-person classroom lesson (but maybe that's to be expected given the class is a very large intro class.)

It is a well-designed study but I have one qualm: I could not figure out from the paper whether the students in the at-home AI tutor group could plausibly have cheated on the post-lesson test with AI. This bothers me enough that I may write to find out. One other thing to keep in mind about these results is that Harvard students already know how to study (at least well enough to get into Harvard) so an AI tutor may be more effective than, say, for younger or less motivated students.
attributes.abstract: Advances in generative artificial intelligence show great potential for improving education. Yet little is known about how this new technology should be used and how effective it can be compared to current best practices. Here we report a randomized, controlled trial measuring college students’ learning and their perceptions when content is presented through an AI-powered tutor compared with an active learning class. The novel design of the custom AI tutor is informed by the same pedagogical best practices as employed in the in-class lessons. We find that students learn significantly more in less time when using the AI tutor, compared with the in-class active learning. They also feel more engaged and more motivated. These findings offer empirical evidence for the efficacy of a widely accessible AI-powered pedagogy in significantly enhancing learning outcomes, presenting a compelling case for its broad adoption in learning environments.

nodes.label: A Meta-Analysis of LLM Effects on Students across Qualification, Socialisation, and Subjectification

attributes.title: A Meta-Analysis of LLM Effects on Students across Qualification, Socialisation, and Subjectification
attributes.summary:
Unlike a lot of other reviews of studies on academic performance, this review also asks about socialization and "subjectification," or the formation of learners as "autonomous and responsible beings." The following results are interesting:
1. Studies are increasing in length (4+ weeks) and LLMs are often used as tutors in a pedagogical framework (versus simply provided as chatbots.)
2. Studies where LLMs acted as active tutors over eight weeks or more saw the biggest gains in academic performance. (I suspect the socialization and subjectification results are not strong enough to mention here.)

This review made it click for me that pedagogically sound LLMs are becoming more common. The authors also point out that *lot* of studies around AI and education right now are about university students in Asia using ChatGPT.
attributes.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly positioned as solutions for education, yet evaluations often reduce their impact to narrow performance metrics. This paper reframes the question by asking “what kind of impact should LLMs have in education?” Drawing on Biesta’s tripartite account of good education: qualification, socialisation, and subjectification, we present a meta-analysis of 133 experimental and quasi-experimental studies ( k = 188). Overall, the impact of LLMs on student learning is positive but uneven. Strong effects emerge in qualification, particularly when LLMs function as tutors in sustained interventions. Socialisation outcomes appear more variable, concentrated in sustained, reflective interventions. Subjectification, linked to autonomy and learner development, remains fragile, with improvements confined to small-scale, long-term studies. This purpose-level view highlights design as the decisive factor: without scaffolds for participation and agency, LLMs privilege what is easiest to measure while neglecting broader aims of education. For HCI and education, the issue is not just whether LLMs work, but what futures they enable or foreclose.

nodes.label: Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build

attributes.title: Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build
attributes.summary:
The authors of this study looked at interactions kids had with ALEKS, an adaptive mathematics learning and assessment platform, before and after the debut of ChatGPT. Some problems kids work on are text-based, susceptible to AI use, while others require interacting with graphics on the screen, making it harder to use AI. The authors looked at the time kids spent on AI-susceptible versus AI-resistant problems in both un-proctored and proctored settings, and found the following:

1. Students spent less time on susceptible problems after the debut of ChatGPT, and the difference disappeared in proctored contexts where AI use would be detected. High school topics showed a cumulative decline of 31.3% over eleven quarters and college-level topics saw a 26.9% decline.
2. There was a 25% cumulative reduction in the odds of a correct response to AI-susceptible retention questions designed to test how well students learned compared to AI-resistant retention questions...but only for proctored retention questions. For un-proctored retention questions, where students could get away with using AI, the likelihood of correct answers increased compared to AI-resistant questions.

This is a really big study! They looked at ten years of data over millions of interactions on the ALEKS platform.
attributes.abstract: How much have students’ ordinary learning processes shifted in response to generative AI, and how does that affect their durable learning outcomes? Self-report surveys show little change, while small-scale behavioral studies report widespread AI use without the scale or duration to measure learning consequences. We address both questions using a ten-year panel of 3.2 million ALEKS learning interactions for investigating time-on-task, complemented by 12.2 million ALEKS PPL placement-assessment response times for examining proctoring and learning outcomes, with a quasi-experimental design exploiting variation in tasks that are more susceptible to AI (text-based word problems) and less susceptible to AI (interactive graph-based problems). Learning time on AI- susceptible problems declines 2.8% per quarter among college students after ChatGPT’s release, cumulating to 26.9% over eleven quarters; high-schoolers show 31.3%, middle-schoolers 9.0%, and Grade 5 students no detectable change. Among college students, the post-ChatGPT divergence vanishes entirely under proctoring, ruling out broad efficiency gains as the likely explanation. Logistic fixed-effects models on randomly assigned proctored retention items yield a 25% cumulative decline in odds of correct response; the same estimator on non-proctored assessment produces a large opposite-signed increase — inconsistent with any platform, cohort, or curriculum explanation. These results are among the first large-scale behavioral and outcome evidence that generative AI has altered how students study and the knowledge they build — the population- level indicator of cognitive surrender, with direct implications for educational research, assessment governance, and AI policy.

nodes.label: Does ChatGPT enhance student learning? A systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies

attributes.title: Does ChatGPT enhance student learning? A systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies
attributes.summary: This review is interesting mainly because it shows some pretty big cracks in what we know about LLMs and student brains. The review finds that, across the included studies, ChatGPT improves academic performance and "higher-order thinking," but they note that a) many studies don't specify if ChatGPT was allowed during performance assessments (and Rismanchian et al. show a drop in performance when it isn't), and b) all of the studies relied on self-reporting for "higher-order thinking" scores...which is notoriously inaccurate.
attributes.abstract: Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (ChatGPT) has generated excitement and concern in education. While cross-sectional studies have highlighted correlations between ChatGPT use and learning performance, they fall short of establishing causality. This review examines experimental studies on ChatGPT’s impact on student learning to address this gap. A comprehensive search across five databases identified 69 articles published between 2022 and 2024 for analysis. The findings reveal that ChatGPT interventions are predominantly implemented at the university level, cover various subject areas focusing on language education, are integrated into classroom environments as part of regular educational practices, and primarily involve direct student use of ChatGPT. Overall, ChatGPT improves academic performance, affective-motivational states, and higher-order thinking propensities; it reduces mental effort and has no significant effect on self-efficacy. However, methodological limitations, such as the lack of power analysis and concerns regarding post-intervention assessments, warrant cautious interpretation of results. This review presents four propositions from the findings: (1) distinguish between the quality of ChatGPT outputs and the positive effects of interventions on academic performance by shifting from well-defined problems in post-intervention assessments to more complex, project-based assessments that require skill demonstration, adopting proctored assessments, or incorporating metrics such as originality alongside quality; (2) evaluate long-term impacts to determine whether the positive effects on affective-motivational states are sustained or merely owing to novelty effect; (3) prioritise objective measures to complement subjective assessments of higher-order thinking; and (4) use power analysis to determine adequate sample sizes to avoid Type II errors and provide reliable effect size estimates. This review provides valuable insights for researchers, instructors, and policymakers evaluating the effectiveness of generative AI integration in educational practice. • ChatGPT enhances academic performance. • ChatGPT boosts affective-motivational states. • ChatGPT improves higher-order thinking propensities. • ChatGPT reduces mental effort. • ChatGPT does not influence self-efficacy.

attributes.title: A New Direction for Students in an AI World: Full report
attributes.summary: This is a great report on AI in education. It focuses on lower education (K-12) but in my opinion much of the findings can be applied to higher education. The authors spoke to 505 people – students, teachers and experts – across 50 countries, and then laid out the potential risks and benefits of AI in the classroom in this "premortem." I would recommend at least reading the executive summary, and perusing the sections based on whatever you're interested in at the moment.
attributes.abstract:
Since the debut of this most common form of generative artificial intelligence, referred to here as “AI,” the education community has been debating its promises and perils. Rather than wait for a decade to conduct a postmortem on the failures and opportunities of AI, the Brookings Institution’s Center for Universal Education embarked on a yearlong global study–a premortem–on generative AI focused on answering the following two research questions:

- What are the potential negative risks that generative AI poses to the education of children and youth?
- Assuming these potential risks, what can we begin to do now to prevent them while maximizing the potential benefits of AI?

This premortem encompassed interviews, focus groups, and consultations with 505 students, teachers, parents, education leaders, and technologists across 50 countries. Our findings are based on their experiences with AI, a close review of hundreds of studies, and a Delphi panel. Given the emergent nature of the field and the need to shed light on how AI is being implemented in education, children’s experiences and those of the adults around them are the focal point. We share our insights not as the final word on AI and education, but as a first vision of where we are already heading.

attributes.title: APA Expert Report on Children’s and Adolescents’ Learning With Educational Technology
attributes.summary: Short, sweet and useful report full of recommendations to educators about how and when to employ educational technologies. Good source of study references, worth a skim if you're curious about the main concerns and implications.
attributes.abstract:
Educational technology (“EdTech”) tools are frequently promoted for their potential to help children and adolescents (ages 5–18) learn, practice skills, and receive support, both at school and at home. Yet a central question remains: can we trust these EdTech tools to fulfill that promise? This report is written for those deciding whether and how to use educational technology tools in K–12 environments: educators choosing EdTech tools, families weighing the adoption of apps, school leaders reviewing purchases, developers designing EdTech tools, and policymakers setting rules.

Research to date shows that EdTech tools are not inherently beneficial or harmful to learners. The effects depend on what an EdTech tool asks the learner to do, how adults integrate it, and the age and needs of the child, and what it replaces. Those conditions are the subject of this report’s recommendations. EdTech tools are changing quickly, vary widely in quality, and are often marketed with claims that run ahead of the evidence. To ensure these EdTech tools effectively serve young people, decisions must be firmly grounded in rigorous scientific evidence rather than marketing promises. By educational technology (“EdTech”), we mean digital tools, platforms, devices, apps, and systems used to support learning and teaching of educational content in the settings where young people learn, including classrooms, homes, tutoring programs, libraries, and after-school settings. Purely recreational technology use, personal smartphone policy, and social media use outside of learning contexts are addressed in other APA health advisories and are not covered here.

nodes.label: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Learners’ Memory: A Systematic Review

attributes.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Learners’ Memory: A Systematic Review
attributes.abstract:
Memory plays a fundamental role in learning through encoding, retention, and subsequent retrieval. The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) in education may reconfigure these processes, yet the field lacks a consolidated account of its impact on learners’ memory. This PRISMA-2020 systematic review synthesizes 26 empirical studies spanning K–12, higher education, and adult learning. Interventions primarily involved large-language-model chatbots and conversational
agents, AI-generated instructional media (teaching videos, mnemonic images), and adaptive analytics-based feedback. Across designs, outcomes were predominantly positive: multiple studies improved immediate retention and demonstrated advantages at delay (one week or course examinations). Benefits were greatest when AI introduced structure (retrieval practice, mnemonic supports), targeted metacognitive or affective feedback, or personalized prompts; negligible effects arose with strong comparison resources or generic, low-presence support. Working memory was seldom assessed, and sensory memory was absent. The evidence synthesized in this study bears implications for educators, policymakers, and learners to adopt AI, align with cognitive principles, monitor delayed outcomes, and ensure ethical implementation.

attributes.title: Google Effects on Memory: Cognitive Consequences of Having Information at Our Fingertips
attributes.abstract: The advent of the Internet, with sophisticated algorithmic search engines, has made accessing information as easy as lifting a finger. No longer do we have to make costly efforts to find the things we want. We can "Google" the old classmate, find articles online, or look up the actor who was on the tip of our tongue. The results of four studies suggest that when faced with difficult questions, people are primed to think about computers and that when people expect to have future access to information, they have lower rates of recall of the information itself and enhanced recall instead for where to access it. The Internet has become a primary form of external or transactive memory, where information is stored collectively outside ourselves.

nodes.label: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task

attributes.title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
attributes.summary: This preprint is cited a **lot** in discussions of LLMs and cognitive offloading. They used EEGs to look at the brains of people writing essays with the help of LLMs, search engines or only their own noggins. Brain connectivity and memory for what participants had written were weakest under LLM assistance. The memory findings are probably the most convincing and useful, as the study design and the EEG findings have been criticized.<Footnote>The main criticisms are the small sample size, the statistical analyses, and the fact that more activity on the EEG doesn't actually tell us much about what's going on in people's brains. The authors themselves acknowledge it is a preliminary study.</Footnote>
attributes.abstract:
With today's wide adoption of LLM products like ChatGPT from OpenAI, humans and businesses engage and use LLMs on a daily basis. Like any other tool, it carries its own set of advantages and limitations. This study focuses on finding out the cognitive cost of using an LLM in the educational context of writing an essay.

We assigned participants to three groups: LLM group, Search Engine group, Brain-only group, where each participant used a designated tool (or no tool in the latter) to write an essay. We conducted 3 sessions with the same group assignment for each participant. In the 4th session we asked LLM group participants to use no tools (we refer to them as LLM-to-Brain), and the Brain-only group participants were asked to use LLM (Brain-to-LLM). We recruited a total of 54 participants for Sessions 1, 2, 3, and 18 participants among them completed session 4. We used electroencephalography (EEG) to record participants' brain activity in order to assess their cognitive engagement and cognitive load, and to gain a deeper understanding of neural activations during the essay writing task. We performed NLP analysis, and we interviewed each participant after each session. We performed scoring with the help from the human teachers and an AI judge (a specially built AI agent).

We discovered a consistent homogeneity across the Named Entities Recognition (NERs), n-grams, ontology of topics within each group. EEG analysis presented robust evidence that LLM, Search Engine and Brain-only groups had significantly different neural connectivity patterns, reflecting divergent cognitive strategies. Brain connectivity systematically scaled down with the amount of external support: the Brain‑only group exhibited the strongest, widest‑ranging networks, Search Engine group showed intermediate engagement, and LLM assistance elicited the weakest overall coupling. In session 4, LLM-to-Brain participants showed weaker neural connectivity and under-engagement of alpha and beta networks; and the Brain-to-LLM participants demonstrated higher memory recall, and re‑engagement of widespread occipito-parietal and prefrontal nodes, likely supporting the visual processing, similar to the one frequently perceived in the Search Engine group. The reported ownership of LLM group's essays in the interviews was low. The Search Engine group had strong ownership, but lesser than the Brain-only group. The LLM group also fell behind in their ability to quote from the essays they wrote just minutes prior. 

As the educational impact of LLM use only begins to settle with the general population, in this study we demonstrate the pressing matter of a likely decrease in learning skills based on the results of our study. The use of LLM had a measurable impact on participants, and while the benefits were initially apparent, as we demonstrated over the course of 4 sessions, which took place over 4 months, the LLM group's participants performed worse than their counterparts in the Brain-only group at all levels: neural, linguistic, scoring. 

We hope this study serves as a preliminary guide to understanding the cognitive and practical impacts of AI on learning environments.

attributes.title: Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry
attributes.summary: Note for this paper – the authors mention "learning outcomes" but really what they mean is how well participants assembled recommendations after researching a topic for 20 minutes. Also, they evaluate "quality" of argumentation by counting how many of seven plausible arguments the participants made after doing research. So it's an interesting study but "learning" and "argumentation" might make you think they tested things they didn't.
attributes.abstract: This study explores the cognitive load and learning outcomes associated with using large language models (LLMs) versus traditional search engines for information gathering during learning. A total of 91 university students were randomly assigned to either use ChatGPT3.5 or Google to research the socio-scientific issue of nanoparticles in sunscreen to derive valid recommendations and justifications. The study aimed to investigate potential differences in cognitive load, as well as the quality and homogeneity of the students' recommendations and justifications. Results indicated that students using LLMs experienced significantly lower cognitive load. However, despite this reduction, these students demonstrated lower-quality reasoning and argumentation in their final recommendations compared to those who used traditional search engines. Further, the homogeneity of the recommendations and justifications did not differ significantly between the two groups, suggesting that LLMs did not restrict the diversity of students’ perspectives. These findings highlight the nuanced implications of digital tools on learning, suggesting that while LLMs can decrease the cognitive burden associated with information gathering during a learning task, they may not promote deeper engagement with content necessary for high-quality learning per se.

nodes.label: From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria

attributes.title: From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria
attributes.abstract: This study evaluates the impact of a program leveraging large language models for virtual tutoring in secondary education in Nigeria. Using a randomized controlled trial, the program deployed Microsoft Copilot (powered by GPT-4) to support first-year senior secondary students in English language learning over six weeks. The intervention demonstrated a significant improvement of 0.31 standard deviation on an assessment that included English topics aligned with the Nigerian curriculum, knowledge of artificial intelligence and digital skills. The effect on English, the main outcome of interest, was of 0.23 standard deviations. Cost-effectiveness analysis revealed substantial learning gains, equating to 1.5 to 2 years of ’business-as-usual’ schooling, situating the intervention among some of the most cost-effective programs to improve learning outcomes. An analysis of heterogeneous effects shows that while the program benefits students across the baseline ability distribution, the largest effects are for female students, and those with higher initial academic performance. The findings highlight that artificial intelligence-powered tutoring, when designed and used properly, can have transformative impacts in the education sector in low-resource settings.

attributes.title: Reader, Come Home
attributes.summary: I haven't had the opportunity to read this book yet, but it looks like an excellent deep dive into why reading (and deep reading in particular) is necessary for critical thinking and other neat things like the stability of democracy.
attributes.abstract:
From the author of Proust and the Squid, a lively, ambitious, and deeply informative epistolary book that considers the future of the reading brain and our capacity for critical thinking, empathy, and reflection as we become increasingly dependent on digital technologies.

This book comprises a series of letters Wolf writes to us—her beloved readers—to describe her concerns and her hopes about what is happening to the reading brain as it unavoidably changes to adapt to digital mediums.

Wolf draws on neuroscience, literature, education, technology, and philosophy and blends historical, literary, and scientific facts with down-to-earth examples and warm anecdotes to illuminate complex ideas that culminate in a proposal for a biliterate reading brain. Provocative and intriguing, Reader, Come Home is a roadmap that provides a cautionary but hopeful perspective on the impact of technology on our brains and our most essential intellectual capacities—and what this could mean for our future.

attributes.title: Teaching with Gemini: Measuring the impact of Guided Learning on student mathematics progress in Sierra Leone
attributes.summary: This is a large randomized control trial with a solid design showing improvement amongst students using Gemini Guided Learning in a classroom setting. A few details for those who have read hype about this study already: The confidence interval was pretty darn wide, the strongest students benefitted the most, and the study is about AI in a carefully-designed, social classroom setting (not "general AI wherever.")
attributes.abstract: We conducted a preregistered randomized controlled trial in Sierra Leone to evaluate the impact of the Guided Learning feature in Gemini on student learning outcomes in mathematics. The trial enrolled 𝑵 = 1763 junior secondary school students across 48 mathematics classrooms. We asked teachers to incorporate Gemini into half of their weekly lessons for eight weeks, adding up to a requested total of 12 hours. Guided Learning significantly improved student learning outcomes, with an intent-to-treat effect of +0.258 SD (𝒑 = 0.029). Uptake exceeded our expectations, with 69.0% of students engaging with Guided Learning for at least 12 hours over the trial. Reaching this threshold yielded a significant treatment-on-the-treated effect of +0.380 SD (𝒑 = 0.029). In focus groups, teachers emphasized students’ enthusiasm for Guided Learning sessions and credited Gemini with helping reveal new ways to teach familiar topics.

attributes.title: The generative AI learning penalty in secondary school
attributes.summary: This is the authors' summary of their academic paper. They looked at AI adoption among 26,811 middle- to high-school students in China and used a staggered difference-in-differences design to estimate the effects of adoption on homework and test scores. They found that time spent on homework went down and homework scores went up after adoption, but *test* scores decreased sharply (20% compared to the pre-adoption average!)
attributes.abstract: Generative AT tools can help students complete assignments faster and achieve better scores. But completing these tasks is not the goal; learning from them is. This column uses data on over 25,000 7th to 12th grade students in China to examine how self-directed use of generative AI affects their learning. Time spent on homework for students who used AI went down and homework scores went up, but their exam scores fell. While the initial effect is small, it grows as students become more proficient with AI tools and as more course material is learned after adoption, suggesting that existing short-duration studies may underestimate the long-run learning costs of using generative AI.

nodes.label: Effects of LLM use and note-taking on reading comprehension and memory: A randomised experiment in secondary schools

attributes.title: Effects of LLM use and note-taking on reading comprehension and memory: A randomised experiment in secondary schools
attributes.summary: I really like this paper because it's one of the few RCTs out there (as of this writing) that looks at a tangible outcome other than academic performance or self-reported measures. They tested students' reading retention, comprehension and free recall with three conditions: LLM use, note-taking or LLM use and note-taking both. Most exciting, they had a gap of three days between learning and test sessions, meaning they were tapping into long-term memory. They found that plain note-taking had the strongest benefit compared to LLM use (though LLM + note-taking was also better for everything except free recall.) And, possibly most fascinating, students perceived the LLM-only condition as less difficult and more helpful than the note-taking condition, even though they did worse.
attributes.abstract: Students' rapid uptake of Generative Artificial Intelligence tools, particularly large language models (LLMs), raises urgent questions about their effects on learning. We compared the impact of LLM use to that of traditional note-taking, or a combination of both, on secondary school students' reading comprehension and retention. We conducted a pre-registered, randomised controlled experiment with within- and between-participant design elements in schools in England. 405 students, aged 14–15 years, studied two text passages and completed comprehension and retention tests three days later. Quantitative results demonstrated that both note-taking alone and combined with LLM use had significant positive effects on retention and comprehension compared to using the LLM alone. Yet, most students preferred using the LLM over note-taking, and perceived it as more helpful. Qualitative results revealed that many students valued the LLM for making complex material more accessible and reducing cognitive load, while they appreciated note-taking for promoting deeper engagement and aiding memory. Additionally, we identified “archetypes” of prompting behaviour, offering insights into the different ways students interacted with the LLM. Overall, our findings suggest that, while note-taking promotes cognitive engagement and long-term comprehension and retention, LLMs may facilitate initial understanding and student interest. The study reveals the continued importance of traditional learning activities, the benefits of combining LLM use with traditional learning over using LLMs alone, and the AI skills that students need to maximise those benefits.

artifacts.label: What Words Are We Using? The "Cognitives"
artifacts.body: Lots of people are talking about human cognition in the context of AI...and we're all using different terms! Even more confusing, sometimes authors define the same terms differently. This is a short-and-sweet summary of the terms I'm seeing most frequently: Cognitive sovereignty, cognitive liberty, cognitive agency and cognitive security. **Cognitive sovereignty**: [Klein and Klein](doc:6abe562e-48cd-44b8-a02f-48f04f710a8e) define cognitive sovereignty as "the enacted behavior of exercising intellectual independence in AI-rich environments, [manifested] as the ability to set goals, validate outputs and appropriately overrule the tool when necessary." Slightly more recently, Konigsberg [defines cognitive sovereignty](doc:4c5b8a1a-132d-460c-838f-8d92de7baa07) as "the capacity to (a) notice when one’s thinking is being displaced, (b) maintain a meaningful connection to how one’s beliefs and judgments are formed, and (c) distinguish between genuine reasoning and the subjective impression of having reasoned." Cognitive sovereignty is the term here that focuses most tightly on the individual and on metacognition: It refers to our ability not only to verify and correct machine thinking, but recognize, describe and protect our own thought processes. **Cognitive liberty**: If cognitive sovereignty is about our capacity to govern our own minds, this term is about our freedom to do so. [Cognitive liberty](doc:32605367-0666-4993-9f78-6adac64dba8f) has conditions: Freedom from interference (e.g., I have the right not to undergo an EEG or take SSRIs); and freedom to self-determine (e.g., I have the right *to* undergo an EEG or take SSRIs.) Cognitive liberty is often invoked in serious legal contexts – think, say, Fifth Amendment-type stuff or whether it is legal to administer drugs to someone to make them able to stand trial. That's probably why Courtney Radsch, a journalist and scholar who applies the term to corporate AI, [uses it.](doc:c70af410-3c1e-4eb2-93c0-d8d385b4c3af) Radsch argues that "a handful of corporations are redesigning the architecture of human thought into a system of cognitive capture" designed to influence everything we see, think and even feel. She further argues that power concentration, surveillance and data capture are the goal of this system and that the only way to protect ourselves is to pass laws protecting freedom of thought. **Cognitive agency**: [Taylor and Krishna](doc:7ae206d8-b677-4570-a419-8dcd48c78ecc) at the Brookings Institution define cognitive agency as "the capacity for people to think and act with AI in ways that increase their control, efficacy and mastery." I really like this definition as it describes cognitive agency along three dimensions: Control, or the "ability to shape the information environment"; efficacy, or the "capacity to act and think effectively with AI to pursue goals"; and mastery, or the "capacity to experience, learn and grow durable capabilities through human-AI interaction over time." Unlike the cognitive sovereignty definitions I've seen, Taylor and Krishna emphasize that cognitive agency can be collective, e.g., collective control over an information environment involves questions of access, portability and interoperability. Their definition takes inspiration from "agency" in the context of human development, where agency is often seen as a necessary condition for empowerment and can be both individual and collective. I think this term lends itself more readily to movements like Public AI than, say, cognitive sovereignty (although I noticed that Konigsberg, whose definition we use above, uses the two interchangeably. I'll also note that cognitive agency, as Taylor and Krishna define it, is a teensy bit circular – control, efficacy and mastery both define and result from cognitive agency?) **Cognitive security**: The more traditional definitions of cognitive security focus on how people can be manipulated or influenced by information, e.g., propaganda and deepfakes. The latest definition from Stanford's Cognitive Security Task Force (CSTF) includes both the manipulation and the person's capacity to withstand it – something closer to cognitive sovereignty. In fact, the CSTF defines cognitive security as "protect[ing] against unauthorized access to and hazardous influence over cognitive processes, such as perception, reasoning, decision-making, learning, and judgment. At its core, cognitive security refers to our ability to maintain **sovereignty** over our inner mental landscape, including our thoughts, feelings, subjective experiences, and dispositions. A cognitively secure world, then, supports **human agency** in deliberation, reflection, and sensemaking." (Emphasis mine.) This feels like a pretty broad definition, especially when you look at how tightly-scoped a term like "cognitive sovereignty" is, but I think that's intentional – the CSTF seems to be positioning "cognitive security" as a term for [multiple fields to rally around](doc:f91c46a2-2410-4719-b168-f5fbebf3824b). The CSTF cites the technical lineage of the term, but then extends it across domains and disciplines to policy, UI/UX design, education playbooks, media literacy, disinformation detection, and so on. I have been thinking of "cognitive security" as including everything from LLM sycophancy to those times Meta served beauty ads to teenage girls who had just deleted selfies. **...and now, a bonus term!** What about "autonomy", either cognitive or human? What is it, and how is it different from agency? Not to turn this into an episode of "I read the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy so you don't have to," but it is complicated. Let's take agency first, because we already have a term ("cognitive agency") that invokes it. The SEP [notes that](doc:06701533-e411-441c-97dc-3468d7e8abb3), though agency most broadly means the ability to act on something – the way that, for example, your cat wakes you up in the middle of the night – the common use of the term implies *intention* (which, ok, having met a cat, maybe the example holds.) More specifically, the standard definition of agency is the capacity to perform intentional actions, which – more or less, with a layman's gloss – is driven by mental states, like desires, beliefs and intentions. The SEP also notes that there can be more "refined" kinds of agency than simply acting intentionally, including *mental agency*, as in over decision-making and remembering, and *epistemic agency*, or the control we have to acquire and revise our own beliefs. This appears to be a very rich area of philosophical scholarship (who'd've thunk?) but the version I've put in my pocket for later is: Humans have stuff in our heads, and we act intentionally based on that stuff, and that is human agency. And if somebody asked me to define "cognitive agency" without having read Taylor and Krishna, I would probably say that it's a combination of the SEP's mental and epistemic agency, an umbrella term that encompasses all the actions we take within our own heads.e.g., remembering, judging, trying out hypotheses, evaluating new information, etc. Now, Taylor and Krishna draw the term "agency" from the work of Amartya Sen and others in the context of international development. Sen defines [agency freedom](doc:01ef5509-8fea-4b70-9b98-9eefd75729b9) as the "freedom to achieve whatever the person, as a responsible agent, decides he or she should achieve." He further breaks this freedom down into effective power (e.g., whether you are actually free to do something) and procedural control (e.g., whether you are actively choosing to do that thing.) For example, suppose I intend to buy milk, but when I get to the store it is too expensive. Sen would say that the price of milk affects my effective power whereas my *decision* to buy milk is about procedural control. I suspect Taylor and Krisha inherit these components, too, though they elide "agency freedom" into just "agency." They might say I have diminished cognitive agency, for example, if the interface I am using is designed to interrupt memory formation despite my intent to remember things. Here's where it gets a bit complicated. Sen's "procedural control", to my ears, sounds a bit like "autonomy." And whether you consider autonomy as a flavor of agency or a separable phenomenon depends on who you read. The SEP describes [personal autonomy](doc:6486cb39-0193-4698-b7f9-f19f9c0bde1b) as the authority over one's own actions, and seems to define it as a *special case* of agency, i.e., "autonomous agency." On the other hand, Brendan McCord, who founded the Cosmos Institute and thinks a lot about autonomy and agency in the age of AI, [argues](doc:163500a9-23d2-443e-94e6-990f76410362) that AI can increase agency (which he defines as the ability to get what you want) while neglecting or even degrading autonomy (which he defines as the ability to judge and decide what you want.) I would smooth out this wrinkle immediately and tell you not to worry about it if I didn't suspect many workshops might degrade into diction sparring. If you subscribe to one set of definitions, then when you say "agency" you not only mean your ability to act but your ability to govern what's in your own head. If you subscribe to another, then "agency" leaves out that critical second part. Does it matter? Well, think about when Meta served beauty product ads to those teenage girls. Using one definition, the ads may have undermined the girls' authority over their own intents and actions, reducing their agency. Using the other, this did not undermine their agency at all – it in fact increased it by offering them options. When we convene workshops and host conferences about what, say, the big labs are doing to us, I'd rather we be discussing what happened than talking past each other. So, who's right? Should we commit to autonomy as a condition of agency or a related but separable thing? At risk of sounding uncharacteristically serene,or cynical – if the philosophers aren't on the same page, I don't see why we ought to try and convince anyone else to change terms I think that's the wrong question. I often remember something Joel Chan, a professor over at UMD, said at a workshop – one where, incidentally, there was a lot of fighting over terms and disciplines. He said he sees people as pointers to the vast universes of everything they know and have worked on, and language as a terribly lossy and insufficient means of communicating those universes. I feel that way about "agency" versus "autonomy": It's less about the words used and more about the context.isn't that always the case! Sen works in the contexts of welfare economics, well-being and famine, and gave his lectures on agency freedom at a time where policymakers didn't always take seriously the difference between having the right to do something and the actual ability to do it. McCord works in the context of generative AI, where the concern is not that we will starve but that optimization will damage our capacity for choice even as it makes better choices than we could. Both are talking about respecting and enabling humans' ability to do things, even things that seem sub-optimal to our own immediate well-being (e.g., Sen's example of jumping into a freezing river to save a drowning person; McCord's example of a young person making mistakes as a form of self-authorship.) Both take freedom very seriously. In that respect, I think it doesn't matter whether their terms overlap or conflict, so long as they mean something to someone and we have a reliable translation function. What is that translation function? Well, let's review. I feel comfortable enough saying that cognitive sovereignty is roughly interchangeable with the "mastery" dimension of Taylor and Krishna's cognitive agency, the "procedural control" aspect of Sen's agency freedom, and even McCord's definition of "autonomy": - cognitive sovereignty ≈ mastery ≈ procedural control ≈ autonomy I'm also okay viewing cognitive liberty as an enabler of cognitive sovereignty, and acknowledge by the transitive property that it is probably invoked in similar places as "autonomy" as well: - cognitive liberty → (cognitive sovereignty ≈ autonomy) Cognitive security is clearly more about the protective posture, and because it's intended as a unifying term, I think it probably doesn't matter much whether they're saying "agency" or "autonomy" (though it will be interesting to see if a favorite floats to the top as the Task Force does more work.) Honestly, everyone's definitions are pretty copacetic except for McCord's claim that agency and autonomy can be separated, which I'm not sure Sen or Taylor and Krishna's definitions agree with. But McCord is making his argument in a context that I think Sen would find familiar: That the relentless machinations of the systems you live in can influence your preferences over time. I doubt anybody would disagree that forces like AI can influence how we think, and to ignore our capacity for self-governance is to miss a huge part of the picture. Worried about diction swinging at your next gathering? Well, honestly, it's not like the philosophers have figured this out either, so if it were me I'd pick a set of terms and go with it. But if you want to be more egalitarian, I propose, like, ten minutes tops of diction negotiation, starting with: 1. What words are people using to describe whether somebody governs their own mind? 2. What words are people using to describe whether somebody can act in the real world in the way they intend? 3. Is one a condition of the other? 4. Repeat if you are also discussing collectives.
