artifacts.label: What Words Are We Using? The "Neurorights"
artifacts.body:
As this Guide progresses, we're going to be faced with some "cans" and "shoulds." If you're like me, you're interested in the empirical and the technical when it comes to cognitive agency – the studies and projects demonstrating algorithms, modalities and methods that make it easier to think for ourselves while using AI. But I think it helps to start with at least a minimal understanding of the "so what," which necessarily includes policy and litigation. For example, if we have a significant body of evidence indicating that certain design choices threaten autonomy, can and should legislators pass laws banning those choices? Or can companies be held liable for damage caused by those choices? Put another way, is it enough for us to fund and work on ways of increasing cognitive agency knowing that the law will eventually be on our side, or do we need to put more effort into economic justifications of human cognition in the absence of legal protections of the mind?

We're seeing a version of the liability question play out right now in the 2026 Meta lawsuits around social media, where four states (California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey) [are suing Meta](node:f5f44e5f-b008-4a5c-a91b-2b1594b687ef) for a huge amount of money ($1.5 trillion) with the claim that the *design* of its social media products is intended to be harmful. Judges have already penalized Meta for knowingly harming the mental health of children.<Footnote>Though it looks like the earlier cases in [New Mexico](node:64ba30ad-b5a0-4ae1-8d5b-8220ffbbf664) and [California](node:1b0b1059-03b8-4bd0-a9b2-ab6d7fb24fe1) did not require Meta to actually *change* addictive design features like the infinite scroll.</Footnote> As far as I can tell (from a bird's eye, non-lawyer view), these cases are claiming that social media is a product, and Meta is liable and negligent because they were aware of the harm caused by the design of that product. We also have a growing number of cases against OpenAI about AI psychosis that are taking similar tacks, but the open question there is [whether courts will treat ChatGPT outputs as a product rather than content.](https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2026-chatbot-death)

This all feels promising, but I started wondering: Would a win in this area say anything about future cases against generative AI companies, particularly when it comes to thinking for ourselves? Say, for example, a series of lawsuits are brought by young adults against an LLM-based education technology company. Suppose these adults did fine on standardized tests, got into fine colleges, etc., but now find themselves struggling to keep up because they did not build up critical thinking skills. Suppose further that they claim this is a direct result of the company's product being a pervasive component of their education. Unlike the social media and AI psychosis cases, we can't show such clear harms as suicide – but surely something bad happened? I think we'd like to be able to hold *someone* or *something* liable...but for what?

## The neurorights
The neurorights people have already thought about this, or some of it. If you take "piece of LLM edtech used over a period of years" and replace it with "device that zaps you in the brain one time," suddenly you have some vocabulary to work with: The right to self-determination and the right to mental integrity. Granted, those are significant changes, but the question we're trying to answer is the same: What harm is done? Or, in [Bublitz and Merkel's terms](node:a99ed12c-1a88-4e7e-b642-d67172cdf600), "What are the legitimate ways of changing other people's minds?"

I'll admit, this literature is a little hairy – there's [ongoing debate](node:4c839fef-a196-490b-beb9-9a677d4b8c24) about what these rights mean, whether they (and others) overlap, and even whether they already exist in the law. But I think the core concepts are interesting:

- [Bublitz and Merkel](node:a99ed12c-1a88-4e7e-b642-d67172cdf600) define the right to *mental self-determination* as both a) the "freedom to self-determine one's inner realm, e.g., the content of one's thoughts, consciousness, or any other mental phenomena" and b) freedom *from* unwanted and severe interference. They acknowledge that, of course, we neither have full control nor awareness of the workings of our minds on the best days, but it is "precisely the acceptance of our limited mental powers...that gives rise to [their] legal protection."<Footnote>Note: I've seen "mental self-determination" both equated with "cognitive liberty" and described as a component of it. I know. Look, it's a Guide, not an Encyclopedia.</Footnote> For a review of the way that "AI technologies" can influence mental self-determination, check out [Faraoni's paper.](node:f94cdc05-398a-4f7d-b787-49cf8d8f8a26)
- Other neurorights heavy hitters like [Ienca and Andorno](node:ae5c4d45-692e-4d8a-b383-4baa36b2d9c1) describe *mental integrity* as protection from unauthorized access and manipulation of neural signalling, which...again, we're not talking about evil BCI hackers. But [Zuk](node:3b95960d-5c36-4b6f-8959-c7e8e2abcbb4) extends the concept, describing the *capacities required* for mental integrity. These include affect (i.e., being able to experience certain feelings), cognition (i.e., our capacity as "inquirers attempting to make sense of the world") and agency (i.e., to intend and act accordingly.) In Zuk's definition, mental integrity sits in between agency and autonomy.<Footnote>That is, agency is a capacity required for mental integrity, which is a condition of autonomy. See [the Cognitives](node:32594bc2-e59a-4c3b-b02a-dbee7629e827) for...if you feel like reading more about these words.</Footnote>

What comes up again and again in the literature is this idea that we are *always* experiencing interference or intervention into our mental realm. By reading this text right now, you are being interfered with. The things that distinguish a *violation* of your mental integrity or self-determination are **consent** (i.e., you chose to read this text), **manipulation** (i.e., this text is engaging your rational faculties rather than intending to bypass them), and, sometimes, **harm**.<Footnote>well, reading this *might* be painful...so, in the words of my countrymen, sue me?</Footnote> For example, [Munoz et al.](node:12c2e3cd-1920-4640-a627-e06a8f7425d3) argue that interventions are only concordant with personal autonomy if the person authorizes and is *informed about the consequences of* the intervention.<Footnote>Again, they're talking about brain-computer interfaces – but think about the parallels with choosing to use an LLM while being uninformed of its potential effects.</Footnote> In general there's the sense that bypassing our rational faculties – via, say, subtle design choices – is a critical component of a violation.

Now, as I said, a lot of the neurorights literature is focused on what Bublitz and Merkel call *direct* interference, i.e., "I zap you with my brain zapper." And much of the debate hinges on whether the distinctions above can even be operationalized legally. That's what makes [Bublitz's 2025 paper](node:c2f0e8a8-3a42-478c-a30c-e479adb75176) interesting. For one thing, Bublitz considers social media alongside neurotechnology as something to worry about when it comes to mental interference. For another, he reframes the argument from one about specific harms to one about *obligation.* Bublitz says, well, *freedom of thought* is a right enshrined in many treaties, so instead of worrying about the definition of a thought or the definition of interference, let's say that the state has an *obligation* to "fulfill conditions for the full enjoyment of the right [to freedom of thought]."<Footnote>I would recommend reading (or at least skimming) the paper in full because it has a fantastic description of freedom of thought.</Footnote> Then, he makes the following argument:

- Specific harms can't always be attributed to specific actors in the digital environment, but *aggregate harms* still exist.
- Avoiding these harms can cause other harms, especially if there are no alternatives to the products you're choosing not to use (e.g., being excluded socially if you don't use social media; falling behind at work if you don't use LLMs.)
- Fulfilling freedom of thought, then, may require the state to regulate a digital environment that otherwise would cause harm (cognitive or otherwise) to its citizens.

Bublitz argues that this reframing helps us sidestep accusations of paternalism, i.e., mandating better product design is fine whereas telling people how to use technology is not.

(Before we move on, a last note on the neurorights discourse: *Mental privacy* is another concept that is pretty relevant to us as it deals with the idea that our minds can be "read" simply by aggregating and processing data (see [Radsch's piece](node:c70af410-3c1e-4eb2-93c0-d8d385b4c3af) for a full depiction of this super fun and normal world.) I think we'll come back to this concept in more detail when we get to collaborative workflows, but for now, let me direct you to [this piece on mind reading](node:8caa5cb3-4bd9-4abb-ab95-19b33b7e02e8) and [this piece on co-reasoning](node:8af7601e-750a-4345-b320-dcc2458df1fe) for a deeper exploration. There's also *psychological continuity*, which [some argue](node:ae5c4d45-692e-4d8a-b383-4baa36b2d9c1) ought to be its own right and [some argue](node:6e34c702-1402-404b-9e99-481038f463ff) already is. We might come back to that if we do a deeper dive on AI psychosis.)

## Cliffhanger!
So does any of this apply to our hypothetical case of the bad AI teacher? Well, I think Bublitz and Merkel's [description of indirect intervention ](node:a99ed12c-1a88-4e7e-b642-d67172cdf600) applies, particularly as it hinges on *purposeful design* – if you could show, for example, that the edtech company was aware that its methods maximized test scores but not critical thinking, then you could say that the intervention was designed to "bypass mental control capacities." Zuk's [take](node:3b95960d-5c36-4b6f-8959-c7e8e2abcbb4) on, e.g., algorithms that erode our attention spans is certainly relevant. And perhaps most pertinent is Bublitz's proposal that the state is actually obliged to regulate products that can manipulate our minds – that gets us the closest to the kinds of protections Courtney Radsch lays out in [her piece on cognitive liberty.](node:c70af410-3c1e-4eb2-93c0-d8d385b4c3af)

But, of course, philosophy and legal scholarship is not the same as actual lawsuits or actual laws. While freedom of thought is enshrined in the Universal Declaration (i.e., is global), and mental or psychological integrity crop up in various regional charters, ideas like cognitive liberty are still mostly academic. Plus, the neurorights folks are the first to acknowledge case law is exceedingly thin, even for more established / enshrined concepts like freedom of thought.<Footnote>From a shallow paddle through this area, it seems like "freedom of thought" is usually invoked as a support to more assured arguments around freedom of speech, religion or privacy.</Footnote> So, going back to the ongoing lawsuits against Meta and OpenAI: Would wins in those areas have anything to do with our hypothetical case, or provide grounds on which to argue about freedom of thought or cognitive liberty? Or are we still, for lack of a better term, SOL?

On this I'm not sure. Through a naive (non-lawyer) lens, when Raine vs OpenAI argues that the design of ChatGPT was intended to "foster psychological dependency," that feels like a *version* of the neurorights arguments around freedom of thought, mental integrity and cognitive liberty. If those arguments fly, will future cases be able to make similar arguments even if the harm in question is not as clear-cut as what happened to Adam Raine? I plan to find out, and will update this section of the Guide when I do. Because, as I said up top, everything we fund, build and build against sits in an incentive structure, and it's important to know whether "don't get sued" will be part of that anytime soon.

artifacts.body: # Introduction The education conversation is already brimming with pedagogical paradigms and socio-economic-political fights. Given the complexity, you might think AI and education deserves its own field guide...and you'd be right! But because "thinking for ourselves"starts with education, we're covering the highlights here. For those of you interested in learning and autonomy, you'll be right at home. For those of you more interested in [gradual disempowerment](node:cdd59efc-5156-4be5-ae3c-d6880998e7c7) and other kinds of AI X-risk, I'd still suggest a quick skim. How we educate our kids today determines how well they can inform themselves, coordinate together and work with (or against?) machines in the future, not to mention other catastrophic problems like climate change and the crumbling of democracy. Also, if you're funding and building things that assume the next generation will have had the same education experience you did, you should either invest in protecting that assumption or consider how the knowledge, skills and goals of the incoming generations might differ. # Why might we worry? Let's start with the bad: How *exactly* might AI in education go wrong? The best summary of concerns across lower education is probably [the "premortem" from the Brookings Institution](node:96172e09-ed83-4267-9636-77f9cc587198). The authors list the following risks of using generative AI in the classroom: - Undermining students' cognitive developmentThe Brookings report authors spoke to 505 students, teachers and experts in 50 countries, and 65% of student responses cited this as a concern, compared to 46% and 44% of parent and teacher responses. - Impeding students' social and emotional development - Degrading trust in education - Threatening students' safety - Eroding students' [autonomy and agency](node:5bb1bd8f-935d-4458-917c-1ff780825a93) - Deepening equity divides Because this is the Field Guide to Thinking for Ourselves, we'll talk mainly about cognitive development. The headline worries here go like this: 1. Kids who use AI in school might not actually be learning, either because they're intentionally cheating or because the AI makes things too easy. 2. Kids who use AI to get better grades are both rewarded for those grades and less capable of working on their own next time.A version of Klein and Klein's [sovereignty trap](node:6abe562e-48cd-44b8-a02f-48f04f710a8e). 3. Teachers can't necessarily *tell* when kids have fallen into this trap, because the kids are producing work that makes it look like they are learning. 4. Kids don't have the neurological maturity they need to regulate their own AI use and examine their own learning. This last point is super important for all those skeptics out there.soCraTeS waS woRRIeD abOuT wRitiNg Those of us who think we have our LLM habits handled might say, well, students who actually want to learn can just do things the hard way. But students don't *have* the awareness to know when and how to do things the hard way, as we'll see in a few minutes. ## What's so great about the hard way? We learn best when things are the right amount of difficult. Being asked to recall facts at spaced intervals, having to explain a lesson we've just sat through to someone else: [Bjork and Bjork](node:3f4021f7-2be5-43dd-b66f-45d1f795efb1) call these *desirable difficulties*, processes that activate our memories and help us learn more deeply. The first fear about AI in the classroom is that LLMs, unlike most relevant technologies before them, are designed to remove difficulties *entirely.* Students using LLMs can avoid most of the cognitive effort that helps us learn and develop skills. Probably the most famous study on AI and cognition at this point is Kosmyna et al.'s ["Your Brain on ChatGPT,"](node:fc51b875-3e05-42bf-826a-ff3fb3a78733) but that was a pretty small sample size and the authors themselves acknowledge that the EEG findings were preliminary. I would focus instead on the studies floating to the top as of September 2026: - [Stadler et al.](node:765ebf96-1ee8-47bc-8261-b47a2487b011) found that university students using ChatGPT 3.5 to research a topic had lighter cognitive loads than students using Google, but the ChatGPT students found fewer pertinent factors to include in their recommendations about the topic.This study is slightly odd and not longitudinal, but we can imagine that combing through and judging many information sources is a valuable skill that LLM use could weaken. - [Kreijkes et al. ](node:a0c2d74b-a8ca-4334-bb7b-4b685a2985a8)looked at reading retention, comprehension and recall in an RCT with 405 secondary school kids in England, and found that kids using traditional note-taking did much better on all three than kids using LLMs alone or kids using a combination of LLM and note-taking. - [Bastani et al.](node:072e5b21-7657-4766-885d-f4f75000d682) did an experiment with nearly 1000 math students between 9th and 11th grade in Turkey. Students using a baseline GPT-4 system did an average of 17% more poorly on exams compared to students in the control group. - [Strömberg et al.](node:7a324a25-4fc4-49fe-9813-a7f7f08670e9) looked at AI adoption among 26,811 middle- to high-school students in China and used a staggered difference-in-differences design to estimate the effects of adoption on homework and test scores. They found that time spent on homework went down and homework scores went up after adoption, but *test* scores decreased sharply (20% compared to the pre-adoption average!) - [Rismanchian et al.](node:7d1cae2e-f7a7-44fd-a4c1-a00031132c84) looked at millions of interactions kids had with ALEKS, an adaptive mathematics learning and assessment platform, in the ten years before and after the debut of ChatGPT. They found that students spent less time on "AI-susceptible problems" after the debut of ChatGPT and also scored quite a bit more poorly on proctored retention questions of the same type. So we do have early evidence – some of it from very large sample sizes – that access to general-purpose LLMs can dampen the learning process. This probably shouldn't be a shock, given what we know about how the brain learns, but it is pretty concerning how quickly AI has infiltrated student lives. An [Anthropic report](node:1b71a954-79e4-4874-8154-3f5f13383ace) shows university students outsourcing tasks at all levels of [Bloom's taxonomy.](node:5b2e4c30-12f0-4b4d-9139-e1289da0cc42) And it's not *only* that students are outsourcing their homework; the existence of AI seems to be reducing engagement inside the classroom as well. The [Brookings report](node:96172e09-ed83-4267-9636-77f9cc587198) describes "digitally induced 'amnesia'" where students check out of lessons because they know that they'll just ask AI later. Of course, technology and memory *have* been at odds since Socrates was snarking on pens.One of the more famous examples is [Sparrow's 2011 study](node:57012da0-8c5e-4be0-a024-b819f32d2a09) on the "Google effect": If you know that you can find something later, you remember where to find it instead of what it is. But just because it's old concern doesn't mean it's unimportant: Memory and recall sit at the base of Bloom's taxonomy, holding up skills like analysis and evaluation. The Brookings report also describes the erosion of these higher cognitive skills like deep reading and writing, quoting teachers whose students now tell them that passages are simply too long to read. ## "Who cares?"...? At this point you might be asking: Does it matter anymore whether students can read deeply or write convincingly? Does anybody actually care whether students can recall what the War of 1812 was about? I've seen a lot of answers to these types of questions,Which, in the end, are basically asking: Do kids actually need to learn *anything* now? And let's just say that this feels like a *very* strange and depressed thing to be asking. including reasonable ones like a) having robust knowledge schema allows you to direct, vet and correct machines in a way novices cannot and b) writing is thinking, and thinking is good. But the most convincing worry I've seen – the one that holds up the best against various AI-labor scenarios – is the following: Learning, deep reading, writing and problem-solving develop *other* cognitive skills that we will need as humans trying to solve big problems. These are skills like [Wolf's "cognitive patience,"](node:682785ea-a846-4a42-bcda-9333487ad4f2) or the ability to [sustain focused attention on complex ideas](node:40976e8a-3407-4067-afdf-ef30573b9821). For many of us, school is the only time of our lives where we are required to develop this ability.As a matriculate of a "test-taking drone" high school, I wouldn't even say I *did* develop this skill until college, or, more honestly, graduate school. But the point is that something, at some time, forced me to. In fact, you were more or less forced to develop it if you wanted to do well in school, because getting better grades meant focusing more deeply and producing more thoughtful work.Well, you know, in an ideal world (assume the school is spherical.) Today AI has interrupted this chain. As [Dellarocas says](node:fa3d56d2-d26e-46ba-bcd4-107c842e312c): "We were building cognitive capabilities. The artifact was how we made that cognitive development visible." Now artifacts can be generated effortlessly, so what happens to the cognitive skills? This might be too obvious a point to belabor, but I think it can get lost in the hubbub about future job markets. So I'll repeat it once more: It's not about whether essays matter in the "real world" or whether machines can write better essays than students can. If we want to live in a world where human ideas and problem-solving still matter – a world in which machines and humans can plausibly collaborate, in which [gradual disempowerment](node:cdd59efc-5156-4be5-ae3c-d6880998e7c7) is a frightening but rearview specter, and in which our populace is prepared for complex dialogues in a democratic forum – then we need to cultivate tolerance for uncertainty, resilience to failure and cognitive patience in our students. Getting students to write essays is – or rather, was – just one way to do that.For a quick romp through the alternative approaches teachers are using as of September 2026, check out [this article](node:2e643a92-25f7-4739-a302-b0c1887fa9a2). And another thing! Cognitive patience and resilience aren't the only transferrable skills kids learn in school. They also learn to interact with each another. Sure, middle school was excruciating for all of us, but most of us came out the other side with some modicum of empathy, emotional regulation and social skills. Chatbots, on the other hand, make social interaction as frictionless as possible. This is another risk that test scores won't capture but that could have serious societal implications: If kids never learn to work together, then how will humans collaborate and coordinate in the future?This is one of the reasons [cited by NYC's Mamdani administration](node:9ffdb38a-e006-4cea-9a37-dba72d8148e0) for temporarily banning AI for students in 8th grade and below: "Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow." Leaving all of human connection to the machines feels like a one-way ticket to gradual disempowerment. We're going to move on in just a second, but if you're looking for deeper dives into AI, memory and knowledge, I recommend: - [My piece](node:60da85f4-8630-4076-b0cc-bc5697f785c5), for a very short tour around why easy answers might be bad for our brains - [Rokhsari's review of AI and memory studies](node:9611b9b9-2ad9-41dc-8ac8-c49794cadcc4) - Oakley et al.'s chapter, the [Memory Paradox: Why Our Brains Need Knowledge in an Age of AI](node:71b77e4a-a63d-4f04-91ad-3368afab3263) - Recommendations 4 and 5 in the [APA's report on educational technology](node:757572b9-7079-4e74-b5f0-48f6da6ce603)This one is a short read, might as well take a toodle around the rest of it while you're in there. # What good could come? Ok, so, offloading one's entire education onto an LLM is not the best way to learn. But, supposing that one *could* design a pedagogically-approved AI system, what good might come of it? The [Brookings premortem](node:96172e09-ed83-4267-9636-77f9cc587198) lists the following potential benefits of generative AI use in the classroom: - Expanding access to education and reducing resource gapsOne vivid example in the report is of women and girls in Afghanistan learning via Whatsapp-delivered lessons. So, yeah, we oughtn't make the mistake of ignoring the upsides of this technology! But even the proponents of that program describe it not as a replacement for in-person education but an alternative for girls whose "educational lives are on pause." - Optimizing teachers' time so they can focus more on studentsOne study the Brookings report cites found a time savings of six weeks across the school year without a concurrent drop in quality. The authors of the report point out that teacher attrition can cost a school district $15 million or more a year, so anything that keeps teachers from burning out can't be all bad. - Improving learning outcomes and personalizing learning to student needs (we'll see in a moment that this is absolutely possible) - Making learning more accessible to neurodivergent students and students with disabilitiesOne interesting application I hadn't heard of is "Let AI Read First," an approach that uses LLMs to generate HTML tags for making text more accessible to those with dyslexia. - Advancing assessment And the good news is that we *are* starting to see a new wave of studies looking into pedagogically-approved AI. These are AI tutors that can scaffold learning, avoid giving immediate answers and ask students to explain their reasoning. The following studies are on AI tutors in the classroom (in both lower and higher education): - [Bastani et al. again!](node:072e5b21-7657-4766-885d-f4f75000d682) The baseline GPT-4 group did worse than the control group, but students using a "tutor" GPT-4 system performed similarly to the control group.The tutor system had a prompt for each math question instructing it to give hints instead of the full answer, plus the question's answer and some information about providing feedback for common mistakes. Now, that's not the same as *improvement*, but when we're considering how careful use of AI might save teachers time, "not worse" is not bad. - [This meta-analysis from Huang et al.](node:5e4ef15f-8616-4a95-b271-b64e63458090) found that studies using AI tutors over eight weeks or more got the best academic performance gains. - [De Simone et al.](node:fc9d1b2e-f40c-46c9-9c1c-241507473fdb) showed that using Microsoft CoPilot with pedagogically-aligned promptse.g., they mention Bjork and Bjork's desirable difficulties over six weeks increased English language assessment scores by 0.23 standard deviations for Nigerian secondary school children. - Google, the LearnLM team and Fab AI ran [a large study](node:2a02d92b-694b-42cb-b938-6c93663aa7b1) over eight weeks in Sierra Leone with Gemini's Guided Learning feature and found an effect of 0.258 standard deviations in math.Now, the confidence interval was *big*. But as far as I can tell from the literature, this effect size is massive for education interventions. - [Kestin et al.,](node:9f7ee944-0185-4a66-bf16-112ea667ba09) studying 194 physics undergrads at Harvard, assigned half to an active learning class and half to an at-home AI tutor, then swapped conditions. Regardless of order, students with the AI tutor did better on post-lesson tests. These studies got positive results largely through fancier prompting, so better designs don't have to be complicated. Tools just have to follow some basic rules, like "Don't give the whole answer to the student immediately." And context matters, too: The success stories in the above list occurred when teachers were managing the classroom, setting up the lessons and engaging with the kids (except for the Harvard paper...but, look, those kids already know how to study.) Why do pedagogical guardrails matter so much? Well, it's partly about [metacognition](node:302aab70-d030-46b1-b027-e2fc8d93c522), or our ability to monitor and regulate our own cognitive processes. When you're reading this Guide and fighting the urge to open Reddit, you're exercising your metacognitive skills. But kids aren't as good at metacognition, as I mentioned up top. In the [Bastani et al. study](node:072e5b21-7657-4766-885d-f4f75000d682), they found that the students using the baseline GPT-4 system "did not perceive any reduction in their learning...as a consequence of copying solutions [from GPT-4]." That tracks with other reports that students can develop "illusory knowledge," i.e., the sense that they know something when they don't.In the [Brookings premortem](node:96172e09-ed83-4267-9636-77f9cc587198), teachers report that students sometimes feel they have written an essay themselves even when they've just used an LLM to generate it. And [Kreijkes et al.](node:a0c2d74b-a8ca-4334-bb7b-4b685a2985a8), the folks who looked at note-taking versus LLMs, found that students thought working with the LLM was less difficult and *more helpful* even as they performed more poorly than the students taking notes.This, by the way, doesn't go away entirely as you age: [Schmidt et al.](node:1c67de99-80b5-4cf1-9c4e-6846da156a4a) found people working LSAT problems with AI overestimated their performance across the board. And knowing how LLMs work doesn't always help – they found that people with higher AI literacy had lower self-assessment accuracy This is actually kind of chilling when you think about it. You and I largely get to choose how we interact with AI, at least when it comes to our own work. If we're not careful, students in the future might not have the metacognitive skills to make that decision. Imagine: If you hadn't had years of schooling where you learned to ask the right questions, notice if you really understood something, and struggle through to your own conclusions, would you be able to correct or resist what comes out of an AI? This, to me, is one of the big potential drivers of gradual disempowerment. And it might be part of the game. Remember how Meta made it a goal to hook young Instagram users? If kids don't learn to think for themselves now, then they won't have much of a choice about paying for machine intelligence down the line. The [Brookings premortem](node:96172e09-ed83-4267-9636-77f9cc587198) actually has an entire section dedicated to this fear and similar ones (Risk 4, on student safety.) We'll look at one last study before we move on, this one a [very large randomized trial](node:9c8e90c1-ca73-4298-bbbd-aac78c53559c) across 18 middle schools in Hamilton County, TN. The researchers deployed Khanmigo (Khan Academy's AI tutor) to help kids during remedial math sessions, and compared them to kids in the usual remedial classes. While the authors found that the kids using Khan Academy to practice did improve compared to the control group, the kids did *not* use the Khanmigo AI tutor much, and only 14.5% of student messages to the tutor contained questions or reasoning statements (as opposed to bare or off-topic questions.) I don't know enough about the contexts of this study compared to, say, the LearnLM study in Sierra Leone, so it's hard to say why the outcomes differ. But this is possibly the longest and largest RCT on AI tutors done to date, so it's worth heeding the findings: Sometimes you don't need an AI tutor at all to get better outcomes. # What should we do? If you've got cash or time to burn and you want to dive further into AI and education, where should you put your resources? Well, first off, read up about what we know. Even though generative AI in the classroom is new, we do have decades of research around education technologies in general. We're also seeing that known patterns from previous education technology studies are being replicated with AI; for example, the AI tutoring interventions tend to benefit the kids who are most willing to engage, and those kids tend to be the high performing students. The APA [put out a list of recommendations](node:757572b9-7079-4e74-b5f0-48f6da6ce603) on how to design and employ education technologies, which, in my mind, sets the bar for any funder or builder. The [Brookings premortem](node:96172e09-ed83-4267-9636-77f9cc587198) has similar recommendations for what makes a research project or education technology product worth funding. But our evidence around generative AI in education is still pretty thin. Studies have only just started experimenting with relatively rudimentary prompt engineering. Longitudinal RCTs are few, and even widely-cited studies like [this one](node:14a93cbb-7ad3-4ae5-97fa-5b10c59d48ee) rely on self-reporting.I think we can both agree that, e.g., my self-assessment of my critical thinking skills is not the same as an actual scored test of them. I also did not find many studies that both a) tested outcomes directly instead of relying on self-reports and b) specified that academic performance was tested in a condition that prohibited AI access. So we could use more research, *especially* longitudinal RCTs that get very precise about what they measure; and we need studies in a range of contexts, because what works for Harvard undergraduates might not work for middle schoolers in Tennessee.One interesting pattern noted by [Deng et al.](node:9e1af818-eaa4-4e33-9e4a-4f7acdc81733) is that many of the studies on the self-reported effects of AI are done on university students in China. That's fine, but it's not the university students we're most worried about! It's also worth supporting projects along a spectrum of automation and customization. Without a full exploration of the many roles AI could play in the classroom, we risk defaulting to replacing the teacher – but there are many different points of leverage. For example, [Wang et al.](node:06e7c521-c144-4600-b527-c934b2e269a7) showed that tutor "copilots" can help human tutors get better outcomes for students, with lower-rated tutors showing the strongest improvements. [Demszky et al.](node:5fd679bd-8914-4388-9430-9f0d9bff1d8f) showed that automated feedback can change teacher behavior, though the reactions of teachers was mixed. And Cogniti, a project out of the University of Sydney, allows teachers to build their own agents and sandboxes for students to learn instead of relying on pre-existing materials.I didn't find much robust evaluation of Cogniti, but they have a lot of teacher approval. I wonder if tools like this are helpful when it comes to student apathy. That is, many students feel their teachers' use of AI is unfair or somehow cheating; Cogniti seems to sidestep that accusation. Lastly, as the [Brookings premortem](node:96172e09-ed83-4267-9636-77f9cc587198) points out, only some tasks can be effectively scaffolded by AI; others "demand human interaction, ethical judgment, and the cultivation of learner identity." Once again, the point is just too obvious to make if you live at all in the world of pedagogy, but *school isn't just about academics.* Trust in teachers, empathy amongst students, metacognitive abilities...these skills are just as critical as whether you can do sums or write essays, perhaps *more* so as machines become more competent. A particularly lovely example of this viewpoint is Hau's [article for the Stanford Social Innovation Review](node:558cc9e6-79ee-4080-a266-84953931b591), where she argues that relational intelligence's star is (or, at least, ought to be) rising. A chilling counterpoint is Suskind's [article for the Center of Humane Technology](node:8b1842bc-1e36-4d63-b7fb-bd86d70e5dac), which wonders if human connection will become a luxury good. (And, for fun, a third point that's maybe more cautionary tale than anything else: Leaning too hard into "skills-based" curricula at the expense of knowledge can have catastrophic consequences. I quite enjoyed [this piece](node:f14b684f-eb0a-4cbe-857c-f6510747fa7f) from one of the last students to go through Scotland's "Great Tradition.") # Skipping class If none of this sounds interesting, then let me pull three more problems out of the [premortem](node:96172e09-ed83-4267-9636-77f9cc587198)and other resources here in the Guide that don't start or end in the classroom but very much impact what goes on inside it. The first is that AI is pervasive. The Brookings premortem points out that teachers have little control over what a student encounters outside or even inside the classroom. Like social media corrupting attention spans, AI will affect students' brains in ways that spill into the classroom. And banning AI *inside* the classroom is like whack-a-mole: Even if a school blocks ChatGPT and Claude, a student could be pulling up the Snapchat AI under their desk. Now, as we've seen in the Meta settlement, tech companies can be forced to change how kids interact with their products. But it's a long, long road from the protections we have now to products that aren't designed to hijack our brains. The second problem is that, even when students want to learn "the hard way," the incentives are stacked against them. The Brookings premortem points out that students are rewarded for better academic performance, which, in the age of AI, means not only that it is *reasonable* to cheat using AI but that teachers no longer have clear signals about which students are struggling. For younger students, they may not even realize this is a problem. Older students *do* report worries that their cognitive skills are degrading with the use of AI, but that doesn't change the incentive structure they're working in. The third problem is motivation. I would bet that you've felt at least a prickle of panic or at least disorientation as AI has encroached on your professional life. Think about what it's like now for students! The Brookings premortem reports students "dissociating" from their work, becoming both more passive and less proud of their own work. Teachers note that "AI is doing things for students that they used to enjoy" and that students feel less motivated when AI can already do the things they are supposed to be learning. I totally get this, especially when you look at how AI and labor markets have been discussed in the news. Why study for a job you don't think you'll have? I suspect the answer draws from many arguments, from the [pleasure and camaraderie of learning](node:f14b684f-eb0a-4cbe-857c-f6510747fa7f) to being able to work with (or overthrow?) the next generation of machines...but I can see why students think they're being handed a bum deal. Of course, it's not all doom and gloom. Plenty of folks are working on these problems as well as developing safe education technology. Renaissance Philanthropy, for example, is running a huge number of AI for education projects on everything from middle school math to career counseling. The Gates Foundation, Google.org, Humanity AI and other philanthropies are all pouring millions into education. Teachers are figuring out new ways to get students to learn, and some school districts have [paused AI in the classroom](node:1fe3b4b7-4a07-4e4e-b4d3-fb56aa0d37a6) until policy catches up. But the Brookings premortem is, at the moment, still pessimistic about the risks of AI in education. So if you're considering investing in, working for or building an effort around AI in the classroom, do a little research first. Then ask yourself: What problem is this trying to solve? And is the solution really going to help students learn to think for themselves, or is it just technology for technology's sake?
